title: SLA Boundary Workbook and Field Readiness Guide
author: Aisha Raman
content:
Overview:
This workbook is designed to be used during pre-install commercial discussions and engineering handoffs for Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) customers. It defines the deployment boundary, negotiable SLA terms, objective operational readiness criteria, and the acceptance test suite used for go/no-go decisions. Use this document to align Sales, Customer Success, Solutions Engineering, and the Customer's infrastructure team before shipment or rollout.

Scope and intent:
- Applies to: VPC-hosted and on-prem deployments using the Redwood control plane or a federated control plane (customer-managed).
- Excludes: Hosted API customers and internal sandbox environments.
- Purpose: reduce ambiguity in SLAs and acceptance tests, limit scope creep, and provide a reproducible operator checklist for field teams.

Key concepts and definitions:
- Deployment boundary: the set of network segments, DNS entries, and authentication trust relationships that Redwood will operate and monitor versus those the customer is responsible for.
- Tenant SLOs: observable latency and availability targets scoped to a tenant’s ingress path and model variant.
- Evidence artifact: a saved synthetic workload run, traces, and telemetry snapshots used to demonstrate acceptance.

1) Negotiable SLA matrix (example):
- The following table is a negotiation template. Replace values per contract.

| SLA Item | Customer Tier A (example) | Measurement Window | Failure Action |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| 95th pct latency (model/generation) | 120 ms / token | 30 days rolling | Credit + failover to lower-cap model |
| Availability (control plane reachable) | 99.95% | 30 days rolling | Incident escalation + root cause report |
| Service restart MTTR | 15 minutes (stateless), 30 minutes (stateful) | per incident | Auto-rollback if >3 incidents/month |
| Telemetry retention for SLO evidence | 90 days | n/a | Extended retention add-on |

Negotiation guidance:
- Latency guarantees should be tied to a concrete model variant, sequence length distribution, and request size. Attach sample payload distributions.
- Availability guarantees differentiate between control plane, data plane (inference nodes), and customer-managed network.
- Credits and remediation steps must be explicit. Avoid language that implies unlimited retries or unconstrained rollouts.

2) Deployment boundary checklist (to be filled with customer):
- Network: list of ingress CIDR ranges, NAT/egress constraints, required ports (gRPC/HTTP), and BGP/peering expectations.
- Identity: IdP metadata, SCIM for service accounts (if used), KMS/HSM integration points, and rotation cadence.
- Storage & artifacts: snapshot locations for model artifacts, PV size expectations, and snapshot S3-compatible endpoints.
- Patching/maintenance windows: weekly and monthly windows, blackout periods for compliance.
- Operator contact list and change control flow.

Sample network boundary snippet (plain text table):
- Allowed ingress CIDR: 198.51.100.0/24 (customer), 203.0.113.0/28 (redwood ops)
- Required outbound ports: 443 (API), 5222 (internal control plane), 9000-9010 (telemetry flush)
- BGP: optional — ASN 64512 announced to customer edge for multi-region failover

3) Operational readiness acceptance tests (objective pass/fail items):
- Connectivity smoke: control plane and data plane HTTP/S gRPC handshake from three customer locations.
- Synthetic latency run: run the supplied synthetic workload for 48 hours, measure 95th/99th latency and token throughput. Evidence: load generator logs + sampling traces.
- KV cache correctness: cold-start and warm-start checks validating identical outputs for a 500-sample prompt set after model swap.
- Failover exercise: simulate a single-zone outage and validate automated fallback to regional replica with <2x latency multiplier for 90% requests.
- Rollback test: perform a dry-run rollback on canary model deployment and assert KV cache state reconciliation completes without data-loss within specified window.

Acceptance test artifacts (required):
- Synthetic workload config (attached), raw logs (gzipped), trace snapshots (zip), Prometheus/metrics snapshots (JSON), and a signed acceptance statement from the customer operator.

4) Telemetry and evidence contract (sampling & retention):
- Required metrics: per-model qps, per-tenant request latency histogram, queue depth, token generation rate, GPU util, memory pressure, and model swap events.
- Traces: capture sampling at 1% for production by default; escalate to 10% during acceptance tests.
- Logs: structured logs for request lifecycle; sensitive fields redacted per PII policy.
- Retention: default 30 days for traces and detailed logs; extendable to 90/365 days via contract.

YAML example (synthetic-workload.yaml):
---
workload_name: acceptance-synthetic-48h
seed_prompts: 1024
concurrency: 32
latency_target_ms: 120
request_distribution: 
  - prompt_length: [32, 128]
    weight: 0.7
  - prompt_length: [129, 512]
    weight: 0.3
---

CLI snippets (operator validation):
- Run a connectivity check:
  curl -s -f -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://controlplane.example.com/v1/health || echo "control plane unreachable"
- Trigger synthetic workload (field kit):
  rl-run --config synthetic-workload.yaml --out evidence/acceptance-logs.gz

5) Upgrade, rollback and constrained operations policy:
- Upgrade windows: suggested 02:00–06:00 local time, with a 2-hour canary period and automatic rollback if error budget consumed.
- State migration: stateful migrations require pre-flight snapshot and post-flight reconciliation; automated migrations off by default unless customer opts-in.
- Rollback escalation: if automated rollback does not complete within 30 minutes, operator-run rollback per documented runbook.
- Safe-mode: when network instability detected, degrade to CPU-only model variant and limit new canaries.

6) Customer-signed operational commitments (checklist for contract appendix):
- Provide a point-of-contact with SRE-level access and commit to change window notifications 48 hours in advance.
- Maintain the agreed BGP/peering or NAT configuration for failover testing.
- Allocate an operator for acceptance test execution and sign-off.

7) Example acceptance run timeline (48h):
- Day 0 (preflight): exchange SSH keys, validate network routes, import model artifact manifest.
- Day 1 (canary): run synthetic workload at 10% of target QPS for 4 hours, evaluate tail latency and error rates.
- Day 2 (full acceptance): ramp to 100% target QPS for 24–36 hours, collect evidence, perform failover and rollback drills.

8) Ownership and escalation path:
- Primary Redwood owner: Solutions Engineering (named engineer on contract).
- Secondary Redwood owner: Customer Success (technical account manager).
- Customer owner: designated SRE/Platform engineer (name and phone/email in contract).
- Escalation timeline: 15 minutes paging for Sev 1, 1 hour for Sev 2, 24 hours for Sev 3 according to the agreed SLO-criticality.

Appendix A — Sample contract clauses (language template):
- Latency SLA: "Redwood will maintain a rolling 95th percentile per-token generation latency of <=X ms for model variant Y, measured over a 30-day window using the agreed synthetic workload distribution. Failure to meet the SLA will entitle the customer to a credit defined at Z% of monthly fee per incident, up to N% per quarter."
- Evidence: "The customer and Redwood will jointly review the evidence artifact set as the authoritative record for SLA calculations. Both parties will attest to artifacts produced during acceptance runs."

Appendix B — Troubleshooting quick links and operator commands:
- Telemetry queries (PromQL examples):
  - 95th latency: hist_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, model))
  - GPU saturation: max_over_time(gpu_utilization_percent[15m]) > 90

Appendix C — Minimal attachments to include in a contract handoff zip:
- synthetic-workload.yaml, acceptance-playbook.md, operator-instructions.sh, signed-operator-acknowledgement.pdf

How to use this workbook in practice:
1. Sales/Solution engineer fills the Deployment Boundary Checklist with customer during discovery call.
2. Customer Success drives SLA negotiation using the Negotiable SLA matrix as a starting point.
3. Solutions Engineering executes preflight and acceptance tests; artifacts are uploaded to the evidence storage agreed in the contract.
4. On successful acceptance, Solutions Engineering issues an acceptance statement and hands over to Customer Success for ongoing account management.

Owner and maintenance:
- Document owner: Aisha Raman (Solutions Engineering liaison to Customer Success).
- Review cadence: biannual or after any major product change affecting deployment boundaries (e.g., new model variants, telemetry changes).

Feedback and improvements:
- If you run this workbook against a new customer and identify missing checks or unclear contractual language, add a ticket to the "private-deploy-contract-templates" board and ping the document owner for inclusion in the next revision.

End of document.
